problem: Modular RL-based ObjectNav systems have many design choices across perception, policy and inference-time tricks, but the standalone contribution of each is not systematically studied, so bottlenecks are unclear and comparisons unfair.
motivation: Modular RL systems generalize and transfer to real robots better than end-to-end ones, but their complexity hides what actually drives performance. Prior work focuses on complex policy networks while perception and test-time heuristics are treated as engineering details.
key_idea: Decompose modular RL ObjectNav into perception, policy and test-time enhancement, ablate each design choice under controlled settings, and combine the best choices into a simple system that sets SOTA on Gibson.
insight: Perception quality (e.g. a Gibson-finetuned Mask R-CNN gives +6.1 SR / +6.7 SPL over default MRCNN for corner policy) and test-time helpers (dynamic goal selection: SPL 43.3 to 47.5 for discrete policy) matter more than policy architecture (CNN vs Transformer gives nearly identical results). Failure analysis attributes 68 of 120 failures to detector errors. Thus policy comparisons are only meaningful once perception and test-time strategies are fixed.
method: Three-module decomposition: perception (detector, map size, map augmentation), policy (observation, action space, network, reward), test-time enhancement (untrapping helper, dynamic goal selection, remapping mask).
Heuristic policies for isolating perception: Corner Goal policy (Stubborn-like with randomness, MOPA-style) and a Frontier policy (FSE-like with random frontier choice).
Detector comparison: Mask R-CNN default vs Gibson-finetuned, RedNet, YOLO11, RF-DETR-Seg, RF-DETR+SAM2, all feeding a top-down semantic map (240 or 480 size, with/without augmentation).

Policy design: PPO-trained long-term goal policy on the top-down map; compressed 3-channel RGB map instead of 20+ channels; ResNet-18 vs ViT-Base; continuous vs discrete corner goals; two reward types (exploration + distance-to-target vs exploration + success + step penalty).

Test-time plug-ins: untrapping helper (alternating turns after repeated collisions), dynamic goal selection (goal collector that switches only when goal reached or unreachable), remapping mask (clear map when stuck in a stair region).
Dynamic-timestep evaluation: max steps = 5 x (D/d + 360/theta), giving D-SR/D-SPL/D-DTS, plus a human expert baseline (5 researchers, same RGB-D and discrete actions).

setting.backbone: Modular: detector (Mask R-CNN Gibson-finetuned etc.) + ViT-Base or ResNet-18 PPO long-term goal policy + local planner
setting.training_data: Policy trained with PPO for 2M frames on Gibson train scenes; detector is the pretrained Gibson-finetuned Mask R-CNN from PONI (no extra data by authors)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + pose, top-down semantic map, goal category
setting.action_space: Habitat low-level discrete (move forward, turn left/right, stop); high-level goal on map (continuous coordinate or 4 corner goals)

results: The final system reaches 84.4 SR / 48.2 SPL on Gibson with the continuous policy (85.3 SR / 47.5 SPL with the discrete policy plus dynamic goal selection), beating NaviFormer (82.6 SR) and T-Diff/HOZ++ (44.9 SPL). Human experts reach 98.0 SR and 53.3 SPL, showing a large gap.
limitations: Mainly evaluated on Gibson with a small set of test scenes; HM3D results are zero-shot and much lower, and MP3D is not evaluated
Test-time helpers and dynamic metrics depend on hand-tuned heuristics; detector errors remain the dominant failure
Simulation only, with no real-robot evaluation
